newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia mining in jeopardy, industry says.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia mining in jeopardy, industry says.

text.p: The future of mining in metal-rich British Columbia is in jeopardy because of sagging profits, low exploration spending and government policies that hinder the industry, a mining association said Wednesday.
A study by Price Waterhouse for the Mining Association of British Columbia found that mining operations in the province made a profit of C$208 million in 1996, down 59 percent from the prior year.

Price Waterhouse consultant Mike Smith said earnings might soften again in 1997 partly because of the closure of one mine and a weaker gold price. Any substantial rise in the Canadian dollar would also hurt earnings.

He attributed the 1996 decline to a sharp drop in world copper prices. Mining has traditionally been one of British Columbia's mainstays and the province is a big producer of copper, lead, zinc and coal.

Gary Livingstone, president of the mining association, said the 1996 results represented an 11 percent after-tax return on investment. While calling this "acceptable," he said "if the industry took another hit this year like the one we took in 1996, we will be deep in red ink."
Moreover, exploration spending of around C$38 million in 1996 was not enough to ensure new mines would be developed. That level is among the lowest of Canadian provinces.
"These levels are insufficient to sustain a viable industry in this province," Louise Lalonde of Price Waterhouse told a news conference.

Industry officials estimated that C$60 million to C$70 million must be spent on exploration to discover one mine and Jack Patterson, managing director of the British Columbia and Yukon Chamber of Mines, said spending of at least C$175 million a year was need to keep the industry healthy in British Columbia.
Because factors like world metal prices are beyond their control, companies urgently need changes in government policies to facilitate their operations, Livingstone said.
He called for greater assurance of access to land, better security of mineral tenure, an easing of the tax burden especially in taxes not tied to profits, streamlining of regulations and other steps.

He said this acceptance of an industry plan could lead to the creation of 22,000 jobs over the next 10 years and that provincial mines minister Dan Miller has so far seem sympathetic to the industry's position.

The British Columbia forestry industry has embraced a similar message and is now negotiating an accord with the province that would target the creation of some 20,000 jobs in the next few years in exchange for streamlining of regulation and paperwork.
